body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

During urine collection for parasitological examination in males, the glans and meatal orifice should be cleaned with…

A. Cotton moistened with 70% alcohol
B. Cotton moistened with cold water
C. Cotton moistened with warm water
D. Dry cotton
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Cotton with 70% alcohol | **F** |
| B. Cotton with cold water | **F** |
| C. **Cotton moistened with warm water** | **T** |
| D. Dry cotton | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Clean with cotton moistened with warm water.
hint: Avoid anything that would kill or distort the organisms.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

For parasitological urine examination (e.g. *Schistosoma haematobium* eggs, *Trichomonas*), the area is cleaned with **plain warm water** only. **Antiseptics and alcohol must be avoided** because they kill or distort motile organisms such as trichomonads and may interfere with the examination.

## Simplified explanation

Use **warm water**, not alcohol, so the parasites are not killed or spoiled.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Diarrhoea mixed with mucus and red blood cells is associated with…

A. Typhoid
B. Typhus
C. Salmonellosis
D. Shigellosis
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Typhoid | **F** |
| B. Typhus | **F** |
| C. Salmonellosis | **F** |
| D. **Shigellosis** | **T** |

> [!answer]
> Shigellosis — bacillary dysentery — classically gives blood and mucus in the stool.
hint: Which one is called dysentery?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Dysentery** means diarrhoea with blood and mucus from invasion and ulceration of the colonic mucosa. *Shigella* invades colonic epithelium (and *S. dysenteriae* type 1 produces Shiga toxin). Typhoid causes systemic illness with fever; typhus is a rickettsial disease with rash and no diarrhoea.

## Simplified explanation

Bloody, mucoid diarrhoea (**dysentery**) points to **Shigella**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The infective stage of *Leishmania tropica* is/are…

A. Amastigote
B. Epimastigote
C. Promastigote
D. Trophozoite
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Amastigote | **F** |
| B. Epimastigote | **F** |
| C. **Promastigote** | **T** |
| D. Trophozoite | **F** |

> [!answer]
> The promastigote, inoculated by the sandfly, is the infective stage.
hint: Which stage lives in the insect vector?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*Leishmania* has two stages: the flagellated **promastigote** in the gut of the female **sandfly** (*Phlebotomus*/*Lutzomyia*), which is injected when it bites, and the non-flagellated **amastigote**, which multiplies **inside macrophages** of the human host. Epimastigotes occur in *Trypanosoma*, not *Leishmania*.

## Simplified explanation

The sandfly injects the **promastigote**; inside us it becomes the amastigote.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The most appropriate laboratory diagnosis for leishmaniasis is/are…

A. Culture of ulcer material or blood
B. Detection of parasites in peripheral blood monocytes
C. Examination of smears taken from infected ulcers
D. Serological examinations
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Culture of ulcer material or blood | **T** |
| B. Detection of parasites in peripheral blood monocytes | **F** |
| C. **Examination of smears from infected ulcers** | **T** |
| D. Serological examinations | **T** |

> [!answer]
> Smears from the lesion, culture and serology are all used; parasites are not routinely found in peripheral blood monocytes.
hint: Sample the lesion itself.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Cutaneous leishmaniasis**: Giemsa-stained smears or biopsy from the **ulcer edge** showing intracellular **amastigotes (Leishman–Donovan bodies)**, plus culture on **NNN medium** and PCR. **Visceral leishmaniasis**: splenic, bone marrow or lymph node aspirate, with serology (rK39 rapid test, DAT). Circulating parasites in peripheral blood monocytes are not a routine finding.

## Simplified explanation

Take a **smear from the sore**, culture it, and use antibody tests.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In a wet preparation, trypanosomes move rapidly with the aid of…

A. An undulating membrane
B. Cilia
C. Flagellum
D. Pseudopodia
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. **An undulating membrane** | **T** |
| B. Cilia | **F** |
| C. **Flagellum** | **T** |
| D. Pseudopodia | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Trypanosomes move by a flagellum and its attached undulating membrane.
hint: Two structures work together.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The trypomastigote has a single **flagellum** arising from the kinetoplast/basal body, running along the body attached to the pellicle to form the **undulating membrane**, and usually emerging as a free anterior flagellum. The rapid lashing motion among red cells in a wet film is a diagnostic feature. Cilia and pseudopodia belong to ciliates (*Balantidium*) and amoebae.

## Simplified explanation

They swim using a **whip (flagellum)** and the **wavy membrane** along the body.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Coccidian parasites that commonly parasitize man include…

A. *Cryptosporidium* spp.
B. *Isospora* spp.
C. *Sarcocystis* spp.
D. *Toxoplasma* spp.
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. *Cryptosporidium* spp. | **T** |
| B. *Isospora* (*Cystoisospora*) spp. | **T** |
| C. *Sarcocystis* spp. | **T** |
| D. *Toxoplasma* spp. | **T** |

> [!answer]
> All four are coccidia of medical importance in humans.
hint: They all belong to the Apicomplexa.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Intestinal and tissue **coccidia** infecting humans: *Cryptosporidium* (watery diarrhoea, severe in HIV), *Cystoisospora belli*, *Cyclospora cayetanensis*, *Sarcocystis* (intestinal and muscular forms) and *Toxoplasma gondii* (definitive host the cat; humans are intermediate hosts). All are **Apicomplexa** with an apical complex and alternating asexual and sexual cycles.

## Simplified explanation

All four — *Cryptosporidium*, *Isospora*, *Sarcocystis* and *Toxoplasma* — are human coccidia.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Stains used in the diagnosis of cryptosporidiosis include…

A. Giemsa
B. Iodine
C. Leishman
D. Modified ZN stain
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Giemsa | **F** |
| B. Iodine | **F** |
| C. Leishman | **F** |
| D. **Modified Ziehl–Neelsen stain** | **T** |

> [!answer]
> Modified (cold) Ziehl–Neelsen — the oocysts are acid-fast.
hint: The oocysts are acid-fast.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*Cryptosporidium* oocysts (4–6 µm) are **acid-fast**, staining bright red against a blue-green background with the **modified (Kinyoun/cold) ZN** method on a concentrated faecal smear. Alternatives: auramine-phenol fluorescence, immunofluorescence, antigen ELISA and PCR. *Cyclospora* and *Cystoisospora* are also acid-fast.

## Simplified explanation

Use the **modified ZN stain** — the oocysts come out red.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The most severe type of malaria is/are caused by…

A. *Plasmodium falciparum*
B. *Plasmodium malariae*
C. *Plasmodium ovale*
D. *Plasmodium vivax*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. ***Plasmodium falciparum*** | **T** |
| B. *Plasmodium malariae* | **F** |
| C. *Plasmodium ovale* | **F** |
| D. *Plasmodium vivax* | **F** |

> [!answer]
> *P. falciparum* causes the severe and potentially fatal form of malaria.
hint: Which species is responsible for cerebral malaria?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*P. falciparum* invades red cells of **all ages**, giving very high parasitaemia, and infected cells **cytoadhere and sequester** in capillaries (PfEMP-1), causing **cerebral malaria**, severe anaemia, acute kidney injury and hypoglycaemia. *P. vivax* and *P. ovale* form **hypnozoites** causing relapses; *P. malariae* may cause chronic infection with nephrotic syndrome.

## Simplified explanation

***P. falciparum*** causes the **most dangerous** malaria.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Characteristics used in the differentiation of *Plasmodium falciparum* on thin films include…

A. Compact gametocytes
B. Distorted infected RBC shape
C. Presence of enlarged infected RBCs
D. Single chromatin dots
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Compact gametocytes | **F** — *P. falciparum* gametocytes are banana/crescent-shaped |
| B. **Distorted infected RBC shape** | **T** |
| C. Presence of enlarged infected RBCs | **F** — enlargement suggests *P. vivax*/*ovale* |
| D. Single chromatin dots | **F** — double chromatin dots (headphone forms) are typical |

> [!answer]
> Only B is characteristic: red cells are not enlarged but may be distorted, with crescent-shaped gametocytes and often double chromatin dots.
hint: Compare with the enlarged cells of *P. vivax*.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*P. falciparum* on a thin film: **normal-sized or slightly crenated/distorted** red cells, delicate **ring forms often with double chromatin dots**, **multiply infected** cells, **appliqué (accolé)** forms at the cell margin, **Maurer's clefts**, absence of mature trophozoites and schizonts in peripheral blood, and **banana-shaped gametocytes**. *P. vivax* shows enlarged cells with Schüffner's dots and compact round gametocytes.

## Simplified explanation

In falciparum the cells are **not enlarged** (may look distorted), rings often have **two dots**, and gametocytes are **banana-shaped**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Antigens targeted for malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) development include…

A. *Plasmodium* aldolase
B. *Plasmodium* lactate dehydrogenase
C. *P. falciparum* histidine-rich protein 2
D. *Plasmodium* aldolase dehydrogenase
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. ***Plasmodium* aldolase** | **T** |
| B. ***Plasmodium* lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH)** | **T** |
| C. ***P. falciparum* histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP-2)** | **T** |
| D. *Plasmodium* aldolase dehydrogenase | **F** — not a real antigen |

> [!answer]
> HRP-2, pLDH and aldolase are the three RDT target antigens; "aldolase dehydrogenase" does not exist.
hint: Three real enzymes/proteins, one invented name.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**HRP-2** is specific to *P. falciparum*, is very sensitive, but **persists for weeks after cure** (and some parasites have *pfhrp2* deletions). **pLDH** and **aldolase** are produced by all species, with pan-specific and species-specific forms, and clear quickly, so they better reflect current infection. Microscopy remains the reference method and allows parasite counting.

## Simplified explanation

Malaria rapid tests detect **HRP-2, pLDH or aldolase**; the fourth name is made up.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Focal areas where tachyzoites of *Toxoplasma gondii* encyst include…

A. Brain
B. Eye
C. Liver
D. Muscles
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. **Brain** | **T** |
| B. **Eye** (retina) | **T** |
| C. Liver | **F** |
| D. **Muscles** (skeletal and cardiac) | **T** |

> [!answer]
> Tissue cysts form chiefly in brain, retina and muscle.
hint: Think of the sites of reactivation disease.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Under immune pressure, rapidly dividing **tachyzoites** convert to slowly dividing **bradyzoites** inside **tissue cysts**, which persist for life in **brain, retina, skeletal and cardiac muscle**. Reactivation in immunosuppression (e.g. advanced HIV) produces **cerebral toxoplasmosis** and **chorioretinitis**.

## Simplified explanation

*Toxoplasma* cysts settle in the **brain, eye and muscles**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The pathogenic stage of *Entamoeba histolytica* in man has:

A. Bull's eye karyosome
B. Cigar-shaped chromatoidal body
C. Ingested RBC
D. Pseudopodia
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. **Bull's eye (small, central) karyosome** | **T** |
| B. Cigar-shaped chromatoidal body | **F** — that is a feature of the cyst, not the trophozoite |
| C. **Ingested RBCs (erythrophagocytosis)** | **T** |
| D. **Pseudopodia** | **T** |

> [!answer]
> The invasive trophozoite shows a central karyosome, ingested red cells and active pseudopodia.
hint: The pathogenic stage is the trophozoite.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The **trophozoite** is the invasive stage: 15–30 µm, with finger-like **pseudopodia** giving progressive motility, a single nucleus with a **small central karyosome** and fine peripheral chromatin, and — diagnostically crucial — **ingested erythrocytes**, which distinguish *E. histolytica* from the non-pathogenic *E. dispar* and *E. coli*. Blunt, **cigar-shaped chromatoid bars** are found in the **cyst**.

## Simplified explanation

The harmful stage is the **trophozoite**, recognised by **red cells inside it**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The most commonly involved area in extraintestinal amoebiasis is/are the…

A. Brain
B. Spleen
C. Liver
D. Lungs
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. Brain | **F** |
| B. Spleen | **F** |
| C. **Liver** | **T** |
| D. Lungs | **F** |

> [!answer]
> The liver — amoebic liver abscess is the commonest extraintestinal form.
hint: Follow the portal blood.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Trophozoites invading the colonic mucosa enter **portal venules** and reach the **liver**, typically the **right lobe**, producing an abscess with "anchovy sauce" contents. Direct extension can then involve the lung or pleura. Serology is usually positive; treatment is **metronidazole** followed by a luminal agent.

## Simplified explanation

Amoebae travel from the gut to the **liver** and cause an abscess.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Infection with *Entamoeba gingivalis* is usually associated with…

A. *Entamoeba coli*
B. *Trichomonas hominis*
C. *Trichomonas tenax*
D. *Trichomonas vaginalis*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. *Entamoeba coli* | **F** |
| B. *Trichomonas hominis* | **F** |
| C. ***Trichomonas tenax*** | **T** |
| D. *Trichomonas vaginalis* | **F** |

> [!answer]
> *Trichomonas tenax* — the other mouth-dwelling protozoan.
hint: Which organisms share the same habitat?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*Entamoeba gingivalis* lives in the **mouth**, in gingival pockets and tartar, and is often found together with ***Trichomonas tenax***, the oral trichomonad. Both are regarded as commensals associated with poor oral hygiene and periodontal disease, have **no cyst stage**, and spread by droplets and kissing. *T. hominis* is intestinal and *T. vaginalis* urogenital.

## Simplified explanation

Both *E. gingivalis* and *T. tenax* live in the **mouth**, so they are found together.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Congenital infection in man is caused by…

A. *Cryptosporidium parvum*
B. *Pneumocystis carinii*
C. *Toxoplasma gondii*
D. *Trichinella spiralis*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. *Cryptosporidium parvum* | **F** |
| B. *Pneumocystis carinii* (*jirovecii*) | **F** |
| C. ***Toxoplasma gondii*** | **T** |
| D. *Trichinella spiralis* | **F** |

> [!answer]
> *Toxoplasma gondii* — one of the classic TORCH agents.
hint: Remember the TORCH group.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Primary maternal infection during pregnancy allows **tachyzoites to cross the placenta**. The classic triad is **chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcification**. Risk of transmission rises with gestational age, while severity falls. Prevention: avoid undercooked meat, cat litter and unwashed produce.

## Simplified explanation

***Toxoplasma*** can pass from mother to unborn baby.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Parasite(s) which produce rectal prolapse in heavy infection, especially among children, is/are…

A. *Capillaria philippinensis*
B. *Toxoplasma gondii*
C. *Trichinella spiralis*
D. *Trichuris trichiura*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. *Capillaria philippinensis* | **F** |
| B. *Toxoplasma gondii* | **F** |
| C. *Trichinella spiralis* | **F** |
| D. ***Trichuris trichiura*** | **T** |

> [!answer]
> *Trichuris trichiura* (whipworm) — heavy infection causes dysentery and rectal prolapse.
hint: The whipworm lives in the large bowel.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Adult whipworms thread their thin anterior ends into the mucosa of the **caecum and colon**. Heavy infection in children causes **Trichuris dysentery syndrome**: chronic bloody mucoid diarrhoea, tenesmus and straining, anaemia, growth retardation and **rectal prolapse**, with worms visible on the prolapsed mucosa. Diagnosis: **barrel-shaped eggs with bipolar plugs** in stool.

## Simplified explanation

Heavy **whipworm** infection makes children strain so much that the rectum prolapses.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

"Nocturnal pruritus ani" is associated with…

A. *Ascaris lumbricoides*
B. *Enterobius vermicularis*
C. *Paragonimus westermani*
D. *Trichuris trichiura*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. *Ascaris lumbricoides* | **F** |
| B. ***Enterobius vermicularis*** | **T** |
| C. *Paragonimus westermani* | **F** |
| D. *Trichuris trichiura* | **F** |

> [!answer]
> *Enterobius vermicularis* (pinworm) — night-time perianal itching.
hint: The pinworm lays its eggs at night.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Gravid female pinworms migrate to the **perianal skin at night** to deposit eggs, causing intense **perianal itching**, disturbed sleep and irritability, and sometimes vulvovaginitis in girls. Scratching leads to **autoinfection** and spread within families and schools.

## Simplified explanation

**Pinworm** causes itching around the anus **at night**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The Graham Scotch tape technique is used for the diagnosis of infection caused by…

A. *Ascaris lumbricoides*
B. *Enterobius vermicularis*
C. *Necator americanus*
D. *Trichuris trichiura*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. *Ascaris lumbricoides* | **F** |
| B. ***Enterobius vermicularis*** | **T** |
| C. *Necator americanus* | **F** |
| D. *Trichuris trichiura* | **F** |

> [!answer]
> The cellophane (Scotch) tape swab is the standard test for pinworm.
hint: Where are the eggs deposited?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Because pinworm eggs are laid on the **perianal skin** rather than passed in faeces, stool examination is usually negative. Clear adhesive tape is pressed to the perianal skin **first thing in the morning before washing or defaecation**, then mounted on a slide: the **D-shaped, flattened-on-one-side** eggs are seen. Repeat on three mornings to improve sensitivity.

## Simplified explanation

Press sticky tape on the skin around the anus in the morning to pick up **pinworm eggs**.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The usual manner of transmission of *Schistosoma* to man is by…

A. An arthropod vector
B. Ingestion of the embryonated egg
C. Skin penetration of the cercariae
D. Drinking of contaminated water
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. An arthropod vector | **F** |
| B. Ingestion of the embryonated egg | **F** |
| C. **Skin penetration by cercariae** | **T** |
| D. Drinking contaminated water | **F** |

> [!answer]
> Free-swimming cercariae penetrate intact skin during contact with fresh water.
hint: Infection happens on contact with water, not by drinking it.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Eggs passed in urine or faeces hatch in fresh water into **miracidia**, which infect **snails**; after asexual multiplication, **fork-tailed cercariae** emerge and **penetrate intact skin**, losing their tails to become schistosomula. Control measures target snails, water contact, sanitation and mass praziquantel treatment.

## Simplified explanation

The larvae **burrow through the skin** when people enter infected fresh water.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Obstructive uropathy is associated with…

A. *Schistosoma haematobium*
B. *Schistosoma japonicum*
C. *Schistosoma mansoni*
D. *Schistosoma mekongi*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. ***Schistosoma haematobium*** | **T** |
| B. *Schistosoma japonicum* | **F** |
| C. *Schistosoma mansoni* | **F** |
| D. *Schistosoma mekongi* | **F** |

> [!answer]
> *S. haematobium* — the urinary schistosome.
hint: Which species lives in the vesical venous plexus?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Adult *S. haematobium* live in the **vesical and pelvic venous plexus**; eggs (with a **terminal spine**) lodge in the bladder and ureteric walls, producing granulomas and fibrosis with **haematuria**, ureteric obstruction, hydronephrosis and a raised risk of **squamous cell carcinoma** of the bladder. The other species are intestinal/hepatic, causing portal fibrosis.

## Simplified explanation

***S. haematobium*** damages the **bladder and ureters**, blocking urine flow.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The region of growth in cestodes is/are the…

A. Neck
B. Proglottid
C. Scolex
D. Strobila
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. **Neck** | **T** |
| B. Proglottid | **F** |
| C. Scolex | **F** |
| D. Strobila | **F** |

> [!answer]
> The neck is the germinative (growth) zone that buds off new proglottids.
hint: New segments are produced just behind the head.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A tapeworm consists of the **scolex** (attachment organ with suckers ± hooks), the unsegmented **neck** (germinative region) and the **strobila** — the chain of proglottids, which mature as they are pushed backwards. Treatment must remove the scolex and neck, otherwise the worm regrows.

## Simplified explanation

Tapeworms grow from the **neck**, just behind the head.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Ocular cysticercosis in man is associated with…

A. *Dipylidium caninum*
B. *Hymenolepis diminuta*
C. *Taenia saginata*
D. *Taenia solium*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. *Dipylidium caninum* | **F** |
| B. *Hymenolepis diminuta* | **F** |
| C. *Taenia saginata* | **F** |
| D. ***Taenia solium*** | **T** |

> [!answer]
> *Taenia solium* — humans can act as intermediate hosts and develop cysticerci in the eye, brain and muscle.
hint: Which tapeworm's eggs are infective to humans?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Ingesting ***T. solium* eggs** (faecal–oral, or autoinfection from an adult worm carrier) releases oncospheres that develop into **cysticerci** in tissues — **neurocysticercosis** (a major cause of epilepsy), subcutaneous and muscle cysts, and **ocular cysticercosis**. *T. saginata* eggs do not cause cysticercosis in humans.

## Simplified explanation

Eggs of the **pork tapeworm** can form cysts in the human eye and brain.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following parasite(s) is/are capable of producing autoinfection in man:

A. *Dipylidium caninum*
B. *Taenia saginata*
C. *Taenia solium*
D. *Hymenolepis nana*
answer:
| Option | Answer |
|---|---|
| A. *Dipylidium caninum* | **F** |
| B. *Taenia saginata* | **F** |
| C. ***Taenia solium*** | **T** |
| D. ***Hymenolepis nana*** | **T** |

> [!answer]
> *T. solium* and *H. nana* can both cause autoinfection.
hint: Which life cycles can be completed within one person?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*Hymenolepis nana* (dwarf tapeworm) needs no intermediate host: eggs hatch in the intestine and develop into cysticercoids in the villi (**internal autoinfection**), producing heavy worm burdens. A *T. solium* carrier can swallow their own eggs (external autoinfection), leading to cysticercosis. *Dipylidium* requires flea ingestion; *T. saginata* eggs are not infective to humans.

## Simplified explanation

The **dwarf tapeworm** and the **pork tapeworm** can reinfect the same person.
